In this video we talk about theta rhythm - a rhythmic pattern of brain activity (4-12 Hz), which is essential for memory encoding and retrieval. 

Spec
items.why_watch: Harvard neuroscience PhD student Artem Kirsanov explains theta rhythm — the 4–8 Hz brain oscillation central to memory formation — and specifically how it may act as a timing signal that sequences memories during learning and sleep. The visualizations are unusually clear, and the video builds toward a genuinely surprising implication about how the hippocampus organizes time.

items.title: We Fired the Most Iconic Sniper Rifles (Over Last 100 Years)
items.description:
How has the sniper rifle evolved over the last 100 years? It's time to find out!

Luke Tomes returns to the Royal Armouries to fire some of the most iconic British sniper rifles of the last 100 years. As always, he is joined by Keeper of Firearms & Artillery, Jonathan Ferguson, who talks him through the history, design and development of each rifle, showcasing how British military sniping has evolved from the battlefields of the Second World War to the modern era.

First up is the Lee-Enfield No
items.why_watch: Royal Armouries curator Jonathan Ferguson walks through a century of British sniper rifle design by actually firing the weapons, which grounds the history in a way that pure documentary narration rarely achieves. If you've ever wondered how sniping shifted from bolt-action WWI precision to modern long-range systems, this is a methodical, well-sourced answer.

items.title: The Battle of Marathon
items.description: The Battle of Marathon was a pivotal event in ancient Greek history that took place in 490 BCE. The Athenians, vastly outnumbered by the invading Persian army, defeated them and secured their freedom from Persian rule. The battle is significant because it marked the first time the Greek hoplite phalanx proved its superiority over the Persian army, establishing the importance of discipline and coordination in warfare. Additionally, the battle has become a symbol of the enduring spirit of freedom
items.why_watch: A compact, straightforward retelling of Marathon that covers the tactical logic of the Athenian double-envelopment maneuver and why it shocked the Persian command. At nine minutes, it's a clean refresher rather than a deep dive — useful if you want the essentials without committing to a full documentary.

discovery_articles.title: Gregg-Crites Octagon House in Circleville, Ohio
discovery_articles.snippet: Located on the southern end of town, the Gregg-Crites Octagon House is one of Pickaway County's most unique architectural landmarks. This eight-sided home in Circleville, Ohio is believed to have been built between 1855-56 by a man named George Gregg. While the exact history is vague, the house may have been constructed to resemble the octagonal courthouse at the center of town when Circleville was originally laid out in the form of a circle.

discovery_articles.title: 15 Best Places to Experience Bioluminescence
discovery_articles.snippet: The humble glow worm is, in fact, a catchall term for numerous glowing creatures, from gnat larvae to fire flys to algae, that can be found all over the world. These tiny critters illuminate the night through bioluminescence, a process in which light is emitted by internal chemical reactions. Bioluminescence has evolved independently in over 90 different species, first emerging some 540 million years ago, and today, it’s still possible to observe the phenomenon firsthand...if you know where to look.

discovery_articles.snippet: The Canary Islands are known primarily as tropical paradise for vacations, but also have beautiful nature and some of the best preserved historical buildings. La Gomerra is a great example of this, with many 15th-century buildings still in use today. Perhaps the most notable of these buildings is the church in San Sebastian which dates back to the early 15th century as a chapel, and was expanded in the following centuries.

news.title: No oven required: Alexina Anatole’s quick and easy no-heat recipes
news.snippet: Cucumber and avocado gazpacho and addictive carrots: when it’s too hot to cook, contrast, texture and seasoning bring dishes to life Heat brings caramelisation, char, the slow collapse of ingredients into something rich and deep, but when it’s too hot to cook, flavour has to be built differently – through contrast, texture and a more deliberate hand with seasoning. Salt, in particular, becomes transformative: drawing out moisture, softening structure, shifting raw into something more yielding. That principle underpins this carrot salad, inspired by the Japanese yamitsuki (‘addictive’) method most commonly used on cabbage, while a chilled cucumber gazpacho offers clean, cooling clarity.
